introduction_markdown:
**GENERAL CERTIFICATE OF EDUCATION BOARD - General Certificate of Education Examination. JUNE 2025, ADVANCED LEVEL. English Language, Paper 2 (0730).**

Answer your questions either exclusively from **PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS)** or from **PART TWO (OLD SYLLABUS)**.

**PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS) - Duration: Two and a Quarter Hours.** Instructions to candidates: ANSWER ONE QUESTION FROM EACH SECTION (Section A: Composition, Section B: Prescribed Texts, Section C: Creative Writing). ALL QUESTIONS CARRY EQUAL MARKS. Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks. Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. A pre-prepared or memorised composition will earn you no marks.

**PART TWO (OLD SYLLABUS) - Duration: Three Hours.** Instructions to candidates: Answer BOTH questions in SECTION A and ONE EACH from SECTIONS B and C in the SAME Answer Booklet, beginning each section on a new page. Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks. Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty. In the SUMMARY question, use mainly your own words. Indiscriminate copying of portions of the passage as your answer will earn you little or no marks. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. A pre-prepared or memorised composition will earn you little or no marks.

**PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS) - SECTION A: COMPOSITION (20 MARKS)**

Mark distribution: Content and Organisation (10 marks); Expression (8 marks); Accuracy (2 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write about from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity. You should write between 500 and 550 words.

questions.enonce_markdown: **a)** Write a story which explains the proverb: 'Don't count your chickens before they hatch'
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. Introduction: a boastful farmer and his hen, and the grandmother's proverb.
2. The farmer spends money he does not have yet (loan, feed, cage, deposit).
3. Climax: only six of fifteen eggs hatch.
4. Consequences: debt, sold goats, loss of respect.
5. Resolution and moral: he changes; the proverb explained in the last paragraph.

**Model composition (532 words)**

In our village of Mbengwi, everybody knew Mr Tanyi as a man who could turn a small hope into a great fortune, at least in his own mouth. He was a poultry farmer of modest means, and the pride of his compound was a brown hen that sat patiently on fifteen eggs behind the kitchen.

On the morning the hen began to sit, Mr Tanyi called his neighbours together. "My friends," he announced, spreading his arms, "within three weeks I shall have fifteen chicks, and within three months fifteen fat fowls. At Christmas I shall sell them at five thousand francs each and buy a motorbike." The neighbours smiled, but my grandmother, who sat shelling groundnuts, only muttered the old proverb: "Do not count your chickens before they hatch."

Mr Tanyi did not hear her. Within days he began to spend money that did not yet exist. He visited the tontine and borrowed one hundred thousand francs, promising to repay it in January. He bought a bag of expensive chick feed and ordered a wooden cage with a zinc roof. He paid a deposit on a motorbike with part of the loan.

On the twenty-first day, the whole village waited in the compound. The hen rose slowly from her nest, but only six eggs had cracked open. Six small, wet chicks wobbled out and tried to stand. Mr Tanyi stared at the remaining nine eggs, which were cold and silent. He broke one open and found nothing but a rotten yolk. He covered his face. The heavy rains and a rat that had visited the nest at night had spoiled the clutch.

The consequences were harsh. Six chicks could never repay a loan of one hundred thousand francs, let alone buy a motorbike. When January arrived, the tontine members came to collect their money, and Mr Tanyi had to sell his two goats and his best radio to pay them. The mechanic kept the deposit because the contract had been signed. Worst of all, the neighbours who had admired his boasting now whispered about it in the market.

One evening, as he fed the surviving chicks, my grandmother crossed the yard and sat beside him. "You were not wrong to hope," she said kindly, "but you were wrong to spend your hope before it was born." Mr Tanyi looked at the small yellow creatures pecking at the millet and nodded slowly. He had learnt a lesson more expensive than any motorbike.

Since then, he has changed. He still keeps hens, but he waits until a chick can stand on its own feet before he speaks of selling it. His small flock grows a little each year. When young men in the village boast about the riches they will earn from some new project, he smiles and quotes the proverb that once made him angry.

That is how our village came to understand the meaning of the saying. A plan is not a result, and a promise is not a profit. Success must first be earned, season after season, before it can be spent. Whoever counts his chickens too early may be left with nothing but an empty nest and a heavy debt.

**Marking grid (the paper prints the split of the 20 marks)**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organisation | 10 | A relevant treatment of the topic as set, a clear introduction, paragraphs that each develop one idea, a logical order and a conclusion |
| Expression | 8 | Varied sentence structures, precise vocabulary, suitable register and tone, good use of linking words, a convincing style |
| Accuracy | 2 | Correct grammar, spelling and punctuation |

**Common mistakes**

1. Writing fewer than 500 or more than 550 words, or ignoring the topic's exact wording (for example listing points instead of telling a story, or giving only one side when asked 'Do you agree?').
2. A weak plan: a long introduction, paragraphs that repeat one idea, no conclusion; or a pre-prepared composition that does not fit the question (it earns no marks).
3. Telling a story without making the proverb's meaning clear: the question says the story must 'explain' the proverb, so the link must be explicit.
